beats.say: Chapter eight built a safety net: a golden set, a calibrated judge, and a gate. Two things slip straight through it.
Planner Copilot can say done, while having changed the wrong warehouse.
And one Tuesday, answers change, although nobody touched the code. Today, we extend the net to agents, and then out into production.
Chapter nine. Testing agents, and shipping safely.
First rule of testing agents.
An agent's final message is a claim. Done! Raised milk safety stock in Pune.
The truth lives in the database. So check the outcome there. Pune: unchanged. And a warehouse in Nashik: changed. The message lied.
Then check the path. The sequence of tool calls is the trajectory. Did it read stock before proposing? Ask for approval before committing? Never touch a delete tool? Stay under twelve steps?
Check rules, not one exact sequence. There's usually more than one good path, and rigid matching punishes good runs.
Planner Copilot passes a task eight times out of ten. Is that good? Think about Arjun. He sends each request once, and dozens a week.
Run the same task k times. Pass at k asks: did at least one attempt succeed? That fits a person picking the best of several, like code suggestions.
Pass to the power k asks: did all of them succeed? That's the one for anything facing customers, or changing data. Watch how fast it falls.
At eighty percent per attempt, three requests in a row all go right only about half the time. A coin flip. That's why consistency matters as much as capability.
So every test run starts in a fresh sandbox. And for conversations, another model plays Arjun, from a scenario card.
Now, the Tuesday mystery.
Tuesday morning. Answers are suddenly longer. A few refuse simple questions. And nobody deployed anything. What would you need to have been recording, already?
A trace for every request. Think of an X-ray: a nested entry for every model call, every search, every tool call. Being able to answer what happened, and why, after the fact, is observability.
Each trace holds the model and its exact version, the prompt version, the chunks and scores, tool calls, tokens, time, cost, and who asked.
Traces hold sensitive data, so mask it, and decide up front how long to keep them.
Then grade live traffic. Run your code checks and calibrated judges on a sample of real requests, every day. These are online evals.
And chart them per group. Here, Bengaluru dropped hard, while the average barely moved. An average hides a regression in one city.

As for Tuesday: answer length and refusals jumped together. That's the signature of a model update. So pin dated model versions, run the regression suite daily, and keep the old version one switch away.
Last: shipping without fear.
Ship in steps. First, offline: the golden set must pass.
Then shadow: the new version answers real questions in parallel, but nobody sees its answers. You compare, with zero risk.
Then a canary: a small group, say five percent of agents in Pune, gets the new version. The success metric and the rollback triggers are written down before it starts.
Something looks off? Roll back. It's a configuration switch, so it takes seconds, not a redeploy.
An A B test answers a different question. Not, does it break? But, is it better? Split by agent, pick one metric in advance, and fix the sample size before you start.
And version everything together. The prompt, the model, the search settings, the index, as one configuration, stamped on every trace.
Let's lock it in.
Check the outcome in the database, not the message.
Check the trajectory with rules.
Pass to the power k: every attempt must succeed.
Observability: a trace for every request.
Online evals watch live traffic, per group.
And a canary goes first, with the rollback ready.
FreshCart is expanding. Six cities, forty franchise partners, two thousand support agents. A million questions a day.
Each franchise must see only its own private documents, plus FreshCart's shared ones.
Leadership wants a forty five minute design review of Ask FreshCart for everyone. How does it scale? How are franchises kept apart? What if the provider goes down? What does it cost?
These are the questions of an LLM system design interview. So, before drawing a single box: what would you need to know, and decide? Write down your first five questions.
That's chapter ten. See you there.
